title: Feeling ill, and body parts as the subject
goal: Describing your symptoms to a pharmacist or doctor — with the Egyptian pattern that makes your body part the subject, not you.
bekal: naming body parts and saying where it hurts
using the وجع pattern, where the body part is the subject
buying medicine at a pharmacy and understanding how to take it

dialogs.title: حوار — في الصيدلية
dialogs.intro: Budi wakes up with a sore throat and a heavy head. He goes into the pharmacy near his home; Egyptian pharmacists are used to handling minor complaints without a prescription.

lines.speaker: الصيدلي:
lines.id: Hello. What's wrong? How are you doing?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: تعبان شوية. زوري بيوجعني من إمبارح.
lines.baca: ta‘baan shuwayya. zōri biywga‘ni min imbaarih.
lines.id: A bit under the weather. My throat's been hurting since yesterday.
lines.literal: tired a-little. throat-my it-hurts-me since yesterday.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.baca: shuwayya bil-lēl. wi raasi kamaan bitiwga‘ni.
lines.id: A little last night. And my head hurts too.
lines.literal: a-little at-the-night. and head-my too it-hurts-me.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.baca: aywa, khuṣuuṣan bil-lēl. wi mabnamsh kuwayyis.
lines.id: Yes, especially at night. And I'm not sleeping well.
lines.literal: yes, especially at-the-night. and not-I-sleep well.

lines.speaker: الصيدلي:
lines.id: Are you allergic to any medicine?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: I don't think so. I've never been allergic to anything.

lines.speaker: الصيدلي:
lines.text: خد الشراب ده تلات مرات في اليوم بعد الأكل.
lines.baca: khud ish-sharaab da talat marraat fil-yōm ba‘d il-akl.
lines.id: Take this syrup three times a day after meals.
lines.literal: take the-syrup this three times in-the-day after the-food.

lines.speaker: الصيدلي:
lines.text: قرص ده لما تحس بحرارة، مش أكتر من أربعة في اليوم.
lines.baca: ’urṣ da lamma tihiss bi-haraara, mish aktar min arba‘a fil-yōm.
lines.id: This tablet when you feel hot, no more than four a day.
lines.literal: tablet this when you-feel with-heat, not more than four in-the-day.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: OK. And should I drink something hot?

lines.speaker: الصيدلي:
lines.text: أكيد. ينسون بعسل وليمون. ده أحسن من أي دوا.
lines.baca: akiid. yansuun bi-‘asal wi lamuun. da ahsan min ayyi dawa.
lines.id: Definitely. Aniseed tea with honey and lemon. That beats any medicine.
lines.literal: sure. aniseed with-honey and lemon. this better than any medicine.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Thanks. What should I do if I don't get better?

lines.speaker: الصيدلي:
lines.text: لو بعد تلات أيام لسه، روح لدكتور. سلامتك!
lines.baca: law ba‘d talat ayyaam lissa, ruuh li-duktuur. salaamtak!
lines.id: If you're still sick after three days, go to a doctor. Get well soon!
lines.literal: if after three days still, go to-doctor. your-safety!

notes: **Body parts as the subject are the most typical feature of Egyptian sickness talk.** راسي بتوجعني literally means "my head is hurting me". English mostly says "my head hurts" or "I have a headache" — the Egyptian pattern always makes the body part the one doing the hurting, with no exceptions.
**Notice that the verb agrees with the gender of the body part.** راس is feminine, so بتوجعني. زور is masculine, so بيوجعني. If two parts hurt, the verb is plural: رجليا بيوجعوني.

**The word خير as a question means "what's wrong? hope all is well".** It isn't empty small talk: Egyptians say it as soon as they see something unusual in your face. If nothing's wrong, just answer خير، الحمد لله.
**The phrase عامل إيه؟ is the casual cousin of إزيك؟** Literally "doing what", it means "how are you". Feminine: عاملة إيه؟, plural: عاملين إيه؟
**The word سلامتك is what you say to someone who's ill**, literally "your safety". The reply is الله يسلمك. When someone sneezes, it's different: يرحمكم الله, answered with يهديكم الله.

**Egyptian pharmacies hand out medicine without a prescription for minor complaints**, and pharmacists often get asked questions like doctors. For medicine that really needs a prescription, they'll say لازم روشتة *rushitta* — from Italian ricetta.

grammars.title: Patterns for pain and feelings
body: Egyptian Arabic has several ways to describe how your body feels, and each has its own pattern that can't be swapped.
after: The first pattern is for **pain in one place**, the second for **an illness or condition with a name**. So عندي صداع and راسي بتوجعني are both correct and mean almost the same thing.
The word حاسس (feeling) is followed by بـ, and it agrees with the person: حاسس، حاسة، حاسين. It's handy for complaints that are hard to name: حاسس إني تعبان.
To ask someone: مالك؟ *maalak?* (what's wrong with you?), وجعك فين؟ *waga‘ak fēn?* (where does it hurt?), بقالك كام يوم كده؟ (how many days has it been like this?).

grammars.title: How to take your medicine
body: Dosage instructions use very fixed phrases, and knowing them lets you read Egyptian medicine packs yourself.
after: The word مرة means "time", and its dual مرتين uses the ـين ending you know from unit five. For three to ten: تلات مرات، خمس مرات.
The word كل here means "every": كل تمن ساعات (every eight hours), كل يوم (every day), كل ساعتين (every two hours).

blocks.text: Almost all body parts in Arabic are **feminine** — عين، ودن، إيد، رجل، ركبة، بطن، راس. It's a rule people rarely mention, yet it's really useful: once you know it, you can pick the right verb form to complain right away.

blocks.title: Body parts in expressions
items: The word عين turns up everywhere: من عنيا *min ‘eneyya* ("from my two eyes", meaning "with pleasure"), عين الحسود (the envious eye).
So does إيد, as in تسلم إيدك (thanks for your cooking or your work), إيده حلوة (his hand brings luck), على إيد فلان (through so-and-so).
The word قلب means both the heart as an organ and the heart as feelings — just like English "heart". قلبه أبيض means "he's kind-hearted".

blocks.text: If it's more than just a cough, these sentences take you from the front door to walking out with a prescription.

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: I'd like to book an appointment with the doctor
it's been like this for three days

blocks.text: The word بقالي means "I've been … for": بقالي تلات أيام (I've been like this for three days), بقالي سنة في مصر (I've been in Egypt for a year). It agrees with the person: بقالك، بقاله، بقالنا. It's one of the most useful patterns in Egyptian Arabic, doing the job of English "have been … for" in a single word.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Egyptian Arabic using the بيوجعني pattern.
items: My throat has been hurting since yesterday.
My back hurts when I move.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right verb form for the gender of the body part.

items: I had a slight fever last night.
I'm not allergic to any medicine.
Take this syrup three times a day after meals.
It's been like this for three days.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: الأكل / بعد / في اليوم / مرات / تلات / خد

answers: راسي بتوجعني. — بطني بتوجعني. — زوري بيوجعني من إمبارح. — ضهري بيوجعني لما أتحرك. — سناني بتوجعني.
أنا تعبان شوية. — كان فيه سخونية شوية بالليل. — ماعنديش حساسية من أي دوا. — خد الشراب ده تلات مرات في اليوم بعد الأكل. — بقالي تلات أيام كده.
زوري بيوجعني من إمبارح. — راسي كمان بتوجعني. — عندك سخونية؟ — خد تلات مرات في اليوم بعد الأكل. — بقالي تلات أيام كده.
